title: Design System Boundary Definition
summary: Design system boundary definition is the practice of deciding where a shared design system stops. It treats refusal as a positive design finding when reuse would misstate task meaning, authority, input conditions, failure interpretation or recovery consequences.

bodySections.heading: Design System Boundary Definition in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy applies design system boundary definition as one of the named practices within its Critical Systems Design method. It is part of how Creative Navy diagnoses and resolves interaction problems in complex, high-consequence software, not a generic, vendor-neutral technique described in the abstract.

bodySections.heading: The Question Design System Boundary Definition Answers
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Design system boundary definition answers one question: what is a design system allowed to make identical. The practice is not a method for building a component library. It is a method for deciding where a shared system stops when products serve different operational purposes.

A design system makes interface elements consistent. In operational portfolios, the hazard is that the same control, with the same appearance, can tell an operator the same thing in two situations where the truth is different. Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats that boundary as a design question, not as a missing asset question. The practice is an instance of constraint respecting because the shared system must preserve the limits carried by task, meaning, authority and consequence.

bodySections.heading: A Shared System Is Tested Where Consistency and Divergence Both Have a Case
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Design system boundary definition is used when a portfolio has a real commercial case for consistency and a real operational case against uniform behaviour. In the Maritime VTS and Portfolio Design System case, the client was a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators. The portfolio covered nine products across Vessel Traffic Services, River Information Services, Voice Communication System and Integrated Communication System families.

The interfaces had been built by separate software engineering teams over many years. The client's request for proposal asked for a common treatment of navigation, menus, tables, data entry, search, panels, dialogues, equipment status, messages and alarms, while preserving functionality and keeping the products appropriate for professional operators.

The operational reason for caution appeared in the radio system. In a general application, a selected state can communicate preference or focus. In the Voice Communication System, an active transmission route also carries equipment state, receive activity, hardware push-to-talk control and potentially time-critical consequence. Creative Navy treated that as evidence that a generic toggle behaviour could not simply be reused.

bodySections.heading: The Six-Gate Reuse Test Defines Direct Adoption, Extension and Refusal
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method used a six-gate reuse test to decide whether a proposed use of a shared component could be adopted directly. The six gates are:

- Task: whether the operator seeks the same outcome as in the source contract.
- Meaning: whether objects, statuses, timestamps and provenance retain equivalent meaning.
- Authority: whether the actor is permitted to trigger the same server-verified transition.
- Input: whether keyboard, mouse, headset and physical control dependencies are equivalent.
- Failure: whether degraded, absent, contradictory or delayed data will be interpreted safely.
- Recovery: whether the user can reverse, correct or reattempt with the same consequences.

All six gates must pass for direct reuse. One failed gate produces a documented extension. A failed gate that would misstate authority or consequence produces an explicit refusal.

bodySections.heading: Disposition Applies to One Use, Not to a Component Family
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Design system boundary definition assigns a disposition to a proposed use in a specific product. It does not classify an entire component family as reusable or non-reusable. The same library component can be adopted directly in one product and refused in another.

The three dispositions are direct adoption, documented extension and explicit refusal. Direct adoption means the documented component contract can be used without changing its operational meaning. Documented extension means the shared component can remain the basis of the design, but the new use must record the difference. Explicit refusal means the shared component would misstate what the user can do, what the system knows or what consequence follows.

bodySections.heading: The Four-Layer Architecture Made the Boundary Test Possible
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The VTS design system used a four-layer architecture. The layers separated primitive values, semantic intent, component behaviour and application composition.

Primitive values covered raw colours, spacing and type scale. Semantic tokens named meaning rather than appearance. Component contracts defined anatomy and valid states. Bounded product compositions assembled documented components for specific operational products.

That separation was the structural precondition for the reuse test. Applications could consume semantic tokens and documented components, but they could not redefine the meaning of a priority colour, overwrite a status label or import radio transmission semantics through a generic action control.

bodySections.heading: Reusable Contracts Carried Eligibility, State and Non-Use Cases
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A reusable component contract in the VTS design system carried a minimum specification. Each contract recorded purpose and eligibility, including explicit non-use cases; an information model with source of truth, identifiers, timestamps, unknown values and permissions; behaviour with triggers, transitions, keyboard focus, interruption and recovery; visual portrayal including accessible text, responsive density and night mode; and quality evidence with accepted scenarios, reviewer and remaining exceptions.

The component system was required to keep eight distinctions apart: vessel and track; track and observation; associated and verified; event time and receipt time; traffic alert and equipment fault; acknowledge and resolve; live and replay; radio resource and transmission. These distinctions made the reuse boundary test concrete. A component could not be reused directly if the proposed use collapsed one of those distinctions.

bodySections.heading: Recorded VTS Results Showed Asymmetry Across Products
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The VTS design-system engagement assessed 70 component applications across four products in the two sprints following detailed design. The Creative Navy-recorded ledger contained 45 direct adoptions, 15 documented extensions and 10 explicit refusals, giving 64.3% direct adoption overall.

The product ledger was uneven. Inland vessel tracking assessed 18 applications, with 13 direct adoptions, 3 extensions and 2 refusals, giving 72.2% direct adoption. Electronic reporting assessed 20 applications, with 15 direct adoptions, 4 extensions and 1 refusal, giving 75.0% direct adoption. Lock planning assessed 17 applications, with 11 direct adoptions, 4 extensions and 2 refusals, giving 64.7% direct adoption. Voice Communications assessed 15 applications, with 6 direct adoptions, 4 extensions and 5 refusals, giving 40.0% direct adoption.

The asymmetry is material. A reuse test that passes every proposed use does not demonstrate boundary control. In this engagement, electronic reporting and Voice Communications produced different results because the operational meaning of the proposed component applications differed.

bodySections.heading: Product Probes Recorded What Should Transfer and What Should Not
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treated each product probe as evidence about the boundary of the shared system. Inland tracking showed that the map-anchored interaction shape transferred, while the truth conditions attached to an inland vessel record could not be imported unexamined. Presenting an administrative waterway notice as a traffic alert would invert the type system, and treating an AIS association as an authoritative registration fact would inflate identity certainty.

Electronic reporting showed that a rejected report and an unfinished draft are different states, so the shared status system had to represent that difference rather than apply the alert lifecycle. Lock planning showed that queue actions retained scheduling semantics, while no interface element was permitted to read as a physical gate command. Voice Communications produced five refusals that prevented inherited behaviour from implying physical transmit authority.

bodySections.heading: Refusal Is a Governance Artefact, Not a Missing Asset
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Design system boundary definition treats an exception as a design finding. In the VTS engagement, a refusal was recorded as a positive result rather than as a gap in the library.

That posture has a governance consequence. A deviation must cite the shared contract, explain the difference in task or authority, and name the approving owner. The point of the record is not to encourage divergence. The point is to make divergence auditable when identical behaviour would be false.

bodySections.heading: Documentation Was Tested by Independent Assembly
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The VTS design system treated documentation as an artefact under test. A client engineer who was not a member of the design team built a working validation-and-correction view for the electronic reporting product in the client's frontend development sandbox. The engineer used 12 documented patterns and 2 domain adaptations, with no additional screen specification from Creative Navy.

Two joint design-and-engineering reviews followed. They checked state interpretation, focus behaviour and documented exceptions, and produced eight adoption observations. Those eight observations did not enter the 36-issue register and did not change it.

The exercise established that an engineer outside the design team could select documented components and assemble a coherent flow unaided. It also established that technology-neutral contracts supplied state, focus, content and recovery rules independently of the underlying component implementation. It did not establish completion of a product migration, an independently certified accessibility result or a production engineering efficiency benchmark.

bodySections.heading: Production Status and Implementation Support Are Limited Claims
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The design system reached production. The client implemented the design system in production. Creative Navy provided regular implementation support across fifteen months, with the client writing the code.

This production status is not a shipped-as-designed claim. No design-fidelity comparison is recorded for the implemented interface. Production also does not establish operational, commercial, training, support or engineering-efficiency outcomes.

bodySections.heading: Evidence Limits Define What the VTS Results Do Not Show
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The 70 assessed applications are usage proposals. They are not components, not shipping software and not additions to the 198 named states. No estimate was made of implementation effort, development cost or velocity.

The engagement does not support a nine-product redesign claim. Four products were designed or probed. Five of the nine products were never designed, and four of those five received only a bounded transfer probe. Integrated Communication System and inland chart management received constraint and applicability reviews only and were not counted in the 70 applications.

The independent assembly exercise was non-production throughout. It demonstrated capability, not completion of a product migration, not an independently certified accessibility result and not a production engineering benchmark.

A measurement framework was specified and handed over for operator efficiency, operator safety and errors, implementation efficiency, system adoption, training and support, and commercial effectiveness. No result from that framework was reported back. The VTS evidence therefore contains no measured reuse outcome, no implementation-effort estimate and no validation that products built through the six gates perform better.
